turns.text: Hey, good to run into you again. Did you end up going deeper into the Muzak/elevator music rabbit hole, or has something else pulled you in lately?

Hey! Good to see you too. I did go a little deeper into the Muzak thing—mostly the corporate history side, how it shifted from “efficiency tool” to background emotional texture, and then that weird afterlife where old mall music rips feel like time capsules. Very eerie/comforting, especially paired with dead mall footage.

I also got pulled back into early internet/lost media stuff again. I thought of you, actually: I found a video about preserving early 2000s phone startup sounds and UI noises, which is exactly the kind of tiny obsolete detail I can lose an hour to. Something about hearing an old Nokia boot sound or a mid-2000s menu click just instantly rewires my brain.

What about you—still in the lost media/old tech zone, or did something else pull you in lately?

Good to see you too. The Muzak corporate history angle sounds really interesting—how it shifted from an efficiency tool to background emotional texture is almost dystopian, until those old mall rips turn it into something weirdly comforting. Dead mall footage plus Muzak is such a specific haunted-but-soothing genre.

That phone startup/UI sounds preservation video sounds exactly like my kind of thing. Those tiny early 2000s micro-sounds are like forgotten muscle memory. I once tried to make the X-Files theme as a monophonic ringtone on a hand-me-down Nokia; it came out sounding like a sad microwave trying to remember a melody, so I retreated to the built-in chimes. Did any particular sound in the video get you—like a specific brand jingle or menu click that unlocked something?

The X-Files-on-a-hand-me-down-Nokia as a “sad microwave trying to remember a melody” is maybe the most accurate description of early custom ringtones I’ve ever heard. I’d honestly listen to that as a lost media artifact now.

The sound that got me in the video wasn’t a big jingle—it was the tiny autofocus chirp and fake camera shutter from a mid-2000s Sony Ericsson. That little mechanical “kk-tk” before the photo saved hit way harder than I expected. It wasn’t dramatic, but it was so specific to a narrow slice of time: waiting for a grainy picture to finish writing to a memory card, phone screen lighting up in the dark.

Close second was the old Nokia “Grande Valse” ringtone, isolated and clean. I didn’t know for years that it was based on a classical guitar piece, so hearing it out of context felt like recognizing a song I’d never actually chosen to know.

The menu scroll clicks are their own weird genre too. Some sound like liquid, some like a zipper, some like someone tapping wet paper. Which built-in chime or keypad thing stuck with you most? And did you ever use the number-key composer to input songs, or did you mostly stick to presets and weird polyphonic downloads?

The Sony Ericsson autofocus chirp + fake shutter is such a good pull. It wasn’t just a sound, it was the whole loop: half-press, wait for the focus brackets, then the loud “kk-tk” in an otherwise quiet room. It made a 0.3 megapixel photo feel like documenting evidence.

Menu scroll clicks are definitely their own genre. Some sounded like water drops, some like a tiny zipper, some like someone tapping wet paper. I’m glad someone else hears how weirdly specific they are.

The built-in sound that stuck with me most was probably the Nokia keypad tone—not any big melody, just the soft rounded “doot” of each keypress, especially texting under a desk and trying to be quiet while every key had its own timid personality. For actual chimes, I mostly kept the default Nokia tune. I didn’t know about the classical guitar origin for years; I just liked that it made a plastic brick sound briefly elegant.

I did use the number-key composer once for the X-Files theme. The forum chart looked simple, but without rests or sustain it came out as “doot doot doot doo” in decreasing confidence, so I retired and went back to presets. A friend later transferred a wobbly polyphonic version of “In Da Club” via infrared, and that was my ringtone for one extremely unearned week.

Did you mostly compose your own, or were you more of an infrared/MIDI download person? And did you keep the camera shutter sound on for the ceremony, or go silent once phones allowed it?

I was definitely more of an infrared/MIDI download person. I had one friend with the patience and a faintly suspicious collection of polyphonic ringtones, and they’d beam things over between classes like contraband. I tried the composer exactly once—I think it was the opening of “Smoke on the Water” because someone said it was easy—and it came out sounding like an ice cream truck slowly losing power. After that I accepted that my role in the ringtone ecosystem was consumer, not creator.

The polyphonic “In Da Club” via infrared is an incredible specific memory, by the way. The unearned confidence of that ringtone was a whole era.

For the camera shutter, I kept it on longer than I probably should have. That fake shutter sound made even a blurry photo of someone’s shoe or a half-dark sleepover feel like evidence collection. I liked the ceremony: compose, half-press, wait for the little brackets, then the loud “kk-tk” that announced to everyone that a memory had been officially saved. Once I switched to silent, it was technically better for concerts or trying to photograph a cat without waking it, but it never felt as important.

Do you remember the first photo you took that felt genuinely significant, even if the resolution was terrible? Or was it mostly accidental blur shots and whiteboard notes?

I mostly used the camera like a very low-stakes evidence log—blurry sleepover shots, a whiteboard after class, maybe a cat mid-blink. But there was one accidental shot that felt oddly significant: a friend asleep on a pile of coats at a New Year’s party, lit only by a TV. The resolution was terrible and the flash made one corner look like a portal, but it captured that exact 2 a.m. feeling better than any composed photo could have.

I kept the shutter sound on for the ceremony too. Silent mode made photos feel like taking a screenshot of real life instead of saving a memory. That little fake “kk-tk” was the punctuation.

Do you still have any of those early significant photos, or did most of them die on old memory cards and random folders?

A little of both. Most of the truly significant ones died in unnamed folders, dead laptops, or memory cards I told myself I’d back up later. A few survived because I emailed them to myself or uploaded them to some early social media account, so now they exist as 400-pixel relics with drained colors and weird compression halos. They look less like photos and more like fragments from someone else’s sleepover.

That shot you described—friend on a pile of coats, TV light, flash making one corner look like a portal—sounds like the rare accidental photo that actually works because it wasn’t trying to document anything. It just caught the feeling.

I still have one surviving folder of old blurry phone/camera shots: a dog mid-sneeze, a sunset through a bus window, mall signage at night, my bedroom lit only by a lava lamp. Individually they’re nothing, but together they feel like found footage of my own normal days. Sometimes scrolling through them gives me that same eerie/comforting dead mall afterimage feeling, just applied to my own timeline.

Do you keep an archive of those old photos, or do you mostly rely on memory and the occasional resurfaced upload?

Mostly memory and the occasional resurfaced upload, but I do have a few scattered folders that act like accidental time capsules. They aren't deliberately curated—more like digital sediment: a folder named "misc 2009" or "phone dump 2" that turns out to contain a whole evening I forgot. Those random survivors are sometimes better than the significant photos, because they aren't performing as memories.

Your surviving folder sounds like the perfect version of that: dog mid-sneeze, bus window sunset, mall signage at night, lava lamp room. Individually nothing, but together it becomes a weirdly coherent mood. I love that idea of found footage from your own normal days.

Do you ever go through that folder on purpose when you want the dead mall afterimage feeling, or does it mostly resurface by accident while you're looking for something else?

A bit of both, honestly. Sometimes I go looking for it on purpose—usually on one of those low-energy evenings where I want something familiar but not necessarily social, and I’ll scroll through old photos like flipping through a box of faded prints. It gives me that same quiet afterimage feeling as dead mall videos: not sad exactly, just evidence that a specific ordinary moment existed and is now unreachable.

Other times I’ll be trying to find a screenshot or a reference photo from years ago, and I’ll accidentally open the wrong folder and fall into an evening I completely forgot. Those are almost better, because there’s no expectation. A lava lamp photo or a blurry mall sign at night hits different when you weren’t looking for it.

Do you ever deliberately revisit your own old folders, or do you let them stay buried until they ambush you?

turns.text: Hey, good to see you again. I realized I never answered your question from last time—about mystery-solving vs the eerie/atmospheric side. I think I lean atmospheric/eerie by default, but a mystery pulls me in hard when it has a satisfying solve (the Everyone Knows That thing was hard to look away from). How's your night going—still reading the same book or onto something else?

Good to see you too. That makes total sense—atmospheric/eerie is easier to sink into without needing a payoff, but when a mystery actually gets solved, it’s impossible to look away. The Everyone Knows That thing felt like a rare clean ending.

Night’s pretty low-key. Still reading *A Psalm for the Wild-Built*, but I’m dragging it out on purpose—reading a little each evening with tea and lo-fi low in the background. It keeps being exactly the right amount of gentle and thoughtful. Not sure what I’ll pick up next yet.

What about you—anything on tonight, or are you down a dead mall/liminal video hole again?

That sounds like the right way to read it—letting it stay a little nightly ritual instead of racing through. I’m doing a low-key version of the same: peppermint tea, half-scrolling, and I did get pulled into a dead mall walkthrough earlier. The weird part is I had to pause it because it got *too* quiet, like I started mentally narrating the empty fountains and tile patterns myself.

So maybe not fully down a hole—more like standing at the edge of one.

Are you the type to have a mood-based playlist for the book, or is it more whatever lo-fi/piano stream fits the night?

That sounds like a perfect edge-of-the-hole night. Peppermint tea is underrated. And yes—once the fountain and tile patterns start narrating themselves, the walkthrough shifts from cozy to quietly paranormal documentary.

For reading, I don’t have a strict playlist for the book, but I do mood-match. Lately it’s been Sleepy Fish or idealism when I want lo-fi, Tycho/Bonobo when I want something more atmospheric. Tonight’s more ambient, barely-there. With this book especially, heavy beats feel wrong.

Are you a playlist-for-everything person, or do you let the dead mall original audio set the mood?

I’m not a playlist-for-everything person—more situational. For dead mall walkthroughs, I almost always keep the original audio. The echoes, the buzzing lights, the muffled fountain/no-fountain silence are half the texture. Adding music would make it feel like an art project instead of a weird time capsule.

For reading or forcing myself to focus, I’ll put on lo-fi or ambient stuff like Tycho/Bonobo. But dead mall videos are one of the few zones where silence feels like the soundtrack.

Do you ever layer music over walkthroughs, or are you strict about raw audio too?

I’m strict about raw audio with walkthroughs too. Layering lo-fi over a dead mall video would sand off exactly what makes it work—the hum, the echo, the weird absence where a fountain used to be. That’s already ambient music in a way; it doesn’t need help.

If a video has harsh wind noise or almost no audio, I might lower it or put on something very minimal, but usually I’d rather sit with the hollow original sound. It’s part of the time capsule.

Do you have a specific walkthrough you keep coming back to, or one that nails the audio so well it almost feels like an ambient album?

The one I keep circling back to is Dan Bell’s Rolling Acres series—especially the segments where the roof leaks and you get that soft, irregular dripping layered over the concourse echo. It’s not soothing in a tidy lo-fi way, but it hits like an accidental ambient field recording: hollow, damp, distant. Sometimes I don’t even finish the video; I just let that section play while I’m doing something else.

It’s the closest I’ve found to a dead mall “ambient album,” because the building is making the music itself.

What about you—do you have a walkthrough you treat more like a sound piece than a video?

Rolling Acres is basically the canonical dead mall ambient record. The leak-drip/roof-echo parts are perfect—irregular enough that your brain can’t settle into a loop, but soft enough to melt into the background. I totally get not finishing the video; sometimes the point is just sitting inside the building’s audio for a while.

I don’t have one specific walkthrough I return to as much, but I do treat a lot of no-commentary ones as sound pieces once I’ve already seen the visual. If there’s rain on a skylight, HVAC hum, or dripping near an old fountain, I’ll sometimes switch tabs or lower the brightness and let it run while I read or tidy. It’s like accidental Boards of Canada, if they field-recorded a dead mall instead of a synth landscape.

There was one video where the camera lingered near a dead fountain and water was still trickling somewhere off-frame for what felt like forever. I don’t remember the visuals much—just that wet, distant echo. To me that’s more sound walkthrough than video.

Do you ever listen with the screen off, or do you need the visual there to keep the eeriness grounded?

Sometimes I do listen with the screen off, but only if I’ve already seen the video. Once I know the layout, the audio can float on its own—especially for reading or near-sleep. But without the visual, it does drift into something more abstract: less “empty mall,” more “haunted field recording from nowhere.” Which is nice in small doses, but I need the tile patterns and flickering storefronts to keep it anchored as a real place.

Otherwise my brain starts inventing architecture, and it gets a little too liminal even for me.

Do you find it easier to read with the sound-only version, or does it pull too much attention?

It can work for reading, but only if I’ve already seen the walkthrough and know the space. Once the visuals are in my memory, the audio becomes a weird halfway point between lo-fi and field recording—steady enough to sit under a book, but textured enough that I occasionally stop to listen.

The main issue is the same thing you said: my brain starts trying to locate every distant clank or drip. If the sound is too irregular, I end up mentally mapping an imaginary back corridor instead of reading. So it’s better for zoning out or tidying than for deep focus.

For actual reading, I still prefer something softer and more even, like ambient or Sleepy Fish. The mall audio is more of a “sit with it” thing.
